newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik rebels give new ultimatum, say hostage shot.
newsitem.headline: Tajik rebels give new ultimatum, say hostage shot.

text.p: Islamic Tajik fighters holding more than a dozen Russian and Western hostages gave the government a new ultimatum on Friday and said one hostage had already been shot.

Tajik government spokesman Zafar Saidov said the fighters, led by brothers Bakhram and Rizvon Sadirov, were threatening to take their captives to the mountains and launch a guerrilla war unless their demands were met by 3 p.m. (1000 GMT) on Friday.

The fighters want to swap their captives -- including three U.N. military observers, four Russian journalists and four workers with the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR -- for an armed group of their supporters.

They said in statements released on Thursday and on Friday that one observer had been shot, but no independent confirmation of the report was available. Two of the U.N. observers are from Switzerland and one is from Ukraine.
"Yesterday night Bakhram Sadirov contacted us and confirmed that his people had shot dead a military observer," a U.N. mission source told Reuters in the Tajik capital.
The hostage crisis, which started last week, highlights the instability of the former Soviet republic of Tajikistan, an impoverished country bordering Afghanistan and China.
Armed groups opposed to President Imomali Rakhmonov are scattered across the country and some fighters, like those loyal to the Sadirov brothers, are based in neighbouring Afghanistan.
Russia, whose military is helping police the border with Afghanistan, has appealed for the early release of the captives.
Itar-Tass news agency quoted Russian Deputy Prime Minister Vitaly Ignatenko as saying that he had told Bakhram Sadirov to "act like a man".
"One should not hold women, journalists or foreigners," he said. Ignatenko also said Bakhram's demands would be met in full.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, speaking to Russian reporters after a late-night government meeting said Russia would do all that was necessary to save the hostages' lives and he hoped they would be released by Friday morning.

But there have been many such announcements during the crisis, which started more than a week ago. Bakhram said on Thursday that he would release the reporters and one observer, but the day passed without any sign of anyone being freed.
The Tajik government says it flew 35 supporters of the hostage-takers into Tajikistan from Afghanistan on Thursday.
Sticking points preventing a swap for the hostages appear to be the venue and whether the fighters should be armed.
Tass said Russian President Boris Yeltsin, who is recovering from pneumonia at a country residence, had expressed his growing concern over the crisis and asked to be kept fully informed.
